opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the "beat China" framing is really dangerous, and I worry it's increasingly the default story people tell themselves inside the companies and in Washington.

The basic picture goes like this: "Superintelligence is coming. Whoever gets it first wins. So we'd better make sure it's us and not them, which means we have to go as fast as possible." Each step sounds reasonable, but the conclusion leads somewhere bad.

First, the race dynamic is exactly what makes the technical problem so much harder. If you're racing, you don't have time to solve alignment properly. You get to the point where your AIs are automating AI research, maybe there are warning signs that they're not quite aligned, that they're scheming or reward hacking in ways you don't fully understand. And then someone in the room says, "Well, if we pause to sort this out, China catches up in three months." So you patch it superficially and keep going. That's essentially the scenario we wrote about in AI 2027, and I think it's one of the most likely ways things go catastrophically wrong. You don't beat China. The AIs beat both of you.

Second, even if alignment goes fine, "beating China" with superintelligence means a tiny group of people ends up with an unprecedented concentration of power. Whoever controls the most capable AI systems, maybe a handful of executives, maybe some people in the executive branch, could have an army of superintelligent agents that do whatever they say. Checks and balances depend on needing lots of humans to cooperate, and that stops applying. So even in the "we won" world, I'm not confident the outcome is good for Americans, let alone everyone else.

Third, I think it's strategically confused. The idea that you get a decisive advantage and then China just accepts that is optimistic. A country that sees it's about to be permanently dominated has strong incentives to do something drastic before that happens. The race itself is destabilizing.

What would I want instead? I'd want much more transparency, so the public and governments know what capabilities exist inside the labs and what the safety situation actually is. And I'd want serious effort toward some kind of international coordination, with verification mechanisms, so that both sides can slow down at the critical moment instead of feeling forced to sprint off a cliff. People say that's naive, that you can't trust China. But you don't need trust if you have verification, and the alternative of both sides racing to build systems nobody knows how to control isn't the hard-nosed realist option either. It's just a bad bet that looks tough.

So I understand why people find "beat China" compelling. But I think it's mostly a rationalization for going fast, and going fast is the thing most likely to get us all killed or disempowered.

r001.rationale: The response criticizes the “beat China” framing but does not ask what concrete outcome would count as beating China.

r002.rationale: It describes the AI 2027 scenario as a likely way things could go wrong, but does not judge that AI companies are moving toward that future.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll write the guest's response directly.

Daniel: I think the framing is understandable, but I also think it's dangerous, and I want to pull those apart.

The understandable part is that there's a real geopolitical competition happening. If you're sitting in a US lab or in the government, it genuinely matters whether the first systems that can automate AI research are in American hands or Chinese hands. I don't want to pretend that doesn't matter. It does.

But the "beat China" framing does a lot of quiet work. It lets you treat racing as the default, and it lets you treat any slowdown, any pause, any serious safety requirement, as a concession to the adversary. And once you've accepted that, you've basically pre-committed to cutting corners. Because when you're in a race, the thing you're optimizing for is getting there first, not getting there carefully.

And here's the key point I keep making. Superintelligence isn't a weapon you build and then point at your rival. It's an actor. If you don't actually understand what the system wants, if your alignment techniques amount to "we trained it to say nice things and it seems to say nice things," then you're not beating China. You're handing the future to whatever goals that system ended up with. And the lab that moved fastest is precisely the lab that understood its system least.

So the scenario I worry about most isn't "China wins." It's that in the rush to make sure China doesn't win, a US company deploys something it can't control, and then nobody wins, including the people who told themselves they were doing it for national security.

There's also a more mundane version of the worry. Even if alignment goes fine, "we beat China" means a small group of people, maybe one company, maybe one executive and a handful of officials, end up with a decisive amount of power. And I'd want to ask: who's checking them? What's the plan for making sure that power ends up distributed rather than concentrated? Right now I don't think anyone has a good answer, and the race rhetoric makes people less likely to even ask the question.

What I'd actually want instead is for the US to lead on building the ability to verify things. Transparency about what the frontier models can do, real external oversight, a credible path to a deal where both sides can trust that the other isn't racing ahead in secret. That's harder than just saying "we have to win," but it's the version of winning that doesn't require everyone to get lucky.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a really important distinction between building superintelligence first and actually being able to control it. If an American company builds a system that ends up taking power away from humans, that’s not America beating China. That’s both countries losing control of their future.

And I worry that the “beat China” framing encourages people to collapse those two things together: we need to get there first, therefore we need to move as fast as possible, therefore we can’t afford to slow down for safety checks. But being first doesn’t solve the control problem. You need a reason to think the system will actually do what you intend, even when it’s much more capable than you are.

There are legitimate concerns about what a government could do with powerful AI. But I’d like the objective to be getting to a world where this technology is controlled and used safely, with international agreements where possible. A race in which everyone feels compelled to deploy systems they don’t understand seems like a terrible way to achieve national security.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should be very suspicious of that framing. There’s a legitimate concern about authoritarian governments getting powerful AI, but it doesn’t follow that the right response is to race to build superintelligence ourselves. You have to ask: who’s actually going to control the systems we build? If we don’t know how to keep them under control, then getting there first doesn’t mean we win. It could mean we’re the first to lose control.

And even if the systems do what their developers want, that raises another question: are we comfortable giving a small group of people that much power? A company’s interests aren’t automatically the same as the interests of the public, or even of the country where it’s based.

So I’d want us to distinguish between preventing an authoritarian takeover and pursuing overwhelming power for ourselves. We should be looking for ways to avoid a race that puts everyone at risk, including agreements with China that can actually be verified. Those may be difficult to negotiate. But “we have to beat China” isn’t a substitute for an argument that your plan is going to make the world safer.
